To play, frolic, or amuse oneself in a free, lively, and joyful way. Think of children splashing in a stream, young animals tumbling over each other, or people dancing carelessly at a celebration — that kind of uninhibited, carefree physical enjoyment is exactly what disport captures.
The most important thing: it's almost always used reflexively

You will rarely see "disport" standing alone. Almost always, you'll see it as "disport oneself" — meaning to give yourself over to play and amusement, to let yourself enjoy freely. The word oneself simply changes to match the subject:

  • The children disported themselves in the shallow water.
  • He spent the afternoon disporting himself in the meadow.
  • She disported herself among the guests at the party.
  • The dolphins disported themselves alongside the ship.

The reflexive form is the standard one. Learn this construction first, and you've grasped the word's most common use.
What makes "disport" different from simply saying "play"?

The word carries more weight than "play." It suggests a kind of carefree, unrestrained enjoyment — where the person (or animal) is completely giving themselves over to the pleasure of the moment. There's a sense of physical energy, movement, and lightheartedness to it. When you say someone disported themselves, you're painting a vivid picture of someone not just passing time, but actively reveling in an activity with freedom and joy.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "The children played on the beach." — simple, neutral, factual.
  • "The children disported themselves on the beach." — vivid and energetic; you can almost see them frolicking, splashing, and running about with complete abandon.

The second sentence is richer. That extra richness is what disport adds.
The tone of the word: formal and literary

Disport is a formal, literary word — and slightly old-fashioned. You won't hear it in everyday conversation. It lives in essays, novels, poetry, and formal descriptive writing. You're most likely to encounter it in older literature (especially prose from the 18th and 19th centuries), nature writing, or in writing where the author is deliberately trying to sound elegant or evocative.

If someone uses it in modern speech, they're either being playfully old-fashioned or deliberately sophisticated. It's the kind of word that gives writing a certain graceful, unhurried quality.

Yes — occasionally. When describing animals or groups in a literary or nature-writing context, some writers drop the reflexive pronoun entirely:

  • Seals disported on the sunlit rocks.
  • Lambs disported in the spring meadows.

The meaning is identical — they were frolicking freely — but even here, you could just as correctly say "disported themselves." The reflexive version remains the dominant and expected form.
A quick note on who or what can "disport"

The word applies equally to:

  • Humans — children, young people, nobles at court, holidaymakers, etc.
  • Animals — dolphins, seals, lambs, puppies — any creature playing freely.

It's especially common when describing creatures in a natural setting, moving and playing with energy.

To disport oneself means to enjoy yourself freely and playfully — usually with physical movement and a spirit of carefree fun — and it's a formal, literary word you'll spot most often in older or carefully crafted writing.
